courseTitle: Ionic - Build iOS, Android & Web Apps with Ionic & Angular

cues.en: How does authentication work in an Ionic app?
An Ionic app typically is a single page application using a front-end framework like Angular but
you could also use React or Vue or build everything with vanilla Javascript
but typically, all the magic happens in the browser,
we're not constantly re-fetching HTML pages. Still of course, we communicate with a server which
has contact to the database where we manage our users and so on and which might also manage our other data
as we're doing it in this course.
Now when we authenticate from our Ionic app, we're sending a request to that server and that request
of course contains things like the user e-mail and password and we expect some response.
Now in a traditional web app where we render all our HTML pages on the server, we would manage authentication
with a session because we always would have a server who which basically knows whether we're authenticated
and so on.
Now however with an Ionic app and a server which is stateless, which is a RESTful API or a GraphQL
API, there a session is not the solution because the server doesn't know us, it doesn't know the client
and it doesn't care about the client,
instead we'll get back a so-called token, which in the end is just a string but a string with a lot of
data encoded into it and that token is generated on the server in a way that only the server can validate
whether that token is valid, which will become important in a second.
So we get that token back after the server determined that our e-mail and password is correct and on
the client, we can save that token in storage and for that of course, I'll show you a how to access storage
that also works on native apps. So we store that token and now the idea behind that token is that whenever
we have to access some protected resource on the server,
so whenever we want to send a request to some endpoint that requires an authenticated user, like for
example when we create a new event, that in such cases we have to attach the token to that request which
we can do because we stored it on the front-end in that storage.
And now the server can check that token and basically find out if it is the token it originally generated
so that we can't send any string,
it has to be that token which we got back and this token is generated in a way that only the server
can tell whether it is valid and that works by using a private key on the server.
So this is the way authentication works.
Now the heavy lifting on the server will be done by Firebase for us here,
if you are building your own server-side solution, you of course will manage that on your own and you
could learn that in courses like my NodeJS, A Complete Guide course if you want to. We'll focus
on the front-end part, on the Ionic app part here.
